implementation_notes: The runtime is a single event loop and every asynchronous completion is delivered on it: an API either returns immediately with a Promise - 'an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation' - or accepts a callback, and async/await (ES2017) makes the waiting linear while rejections carry the error channel. Promise settling is idempotent, so the exactly-once obligation is enforced by the language instead of by convention; use this for one caller and one result, and the EventTarget/EventEmitter variant for multi-subscriber streams.
pitfalls: An unhandled rejection terminates the Node process by default (and is only a console warning in browsers) - always attach a handler, even for calls whose result is ignored.
Promises are single-shot: wrapping an event that can fire repeatedly in one Promise silently drops every completion after the first.
await of an already-rejected promise still needs try/catch; omitting it lands on the same unhandled-rejection path.

variants.name: Completion event on an EventTarget/EventEmitter operation object
variants.implementation_notes: The event-shaped realization the pattern is named for: the operation object emits a named completion event - and usually progress/error events - and the caller subscribes; EventTarget in the DOM and EventEmitter in Node are the runtime primitives ('much of the Node.js core API is built around an idiomatic asynchronous event-driven architecture in which certain kinds of objects emit named events'). Choose it when several parties observe completion or progress, or when the API must stay callback-compatible; prefer the promise form for one caller and one result.
pitfalls: Completion events are not exactly-once by themselves: a listener added after emission never runs, and a listener added twice runs twice per emission.
Per-operation listeners on a long-lived emitter leak the subscriber unless removed - use { once: true }/once()/AbortSignal - and Node's 'error' event throws when it has no listener.
Emission is synchronous in Node's EventEmitter: a slow listener blocks the loop and delays every other completion.
